summary.method: Same prompt, schema, maths and risk checks as the live desk. Point-in-time inputs only. Entry at the first daily close after the news; stops/targets checked on daily closes; round-trip costs charged. Book P&L = R x risk% of book.
summary.caveat: The model may already know how these events played out from its training data, which would flatter these results. Treat this as a test of the machinery and of calibration; the live paper record is the only truly unseen test.

rows.title: Four tankers sabotaged off Fujairah
rows.regime: Elevated Gulf maritime risk after an unverified breaking report of four tankers sabotaged off Fujairah; no confirmed price reaction or independent corroboration.
rows.noTrade: No base rate exists (n=0 for shipping and escalation families), the headline is unverified with no named source, no live AIS data is available, and no post-news prices are provided to judge whether the move is already priced in. Expected value cannot be positively established under honest probabilities, so no trade.

rows.title: Front Altair and Kokuka Courageous attacked in the Gulf of Oman
rows.regime: Fresh Gulf of Oman tanker-attack shock with unconfirmed attribution, and no post-news price data in the input.
rows.noTrade: Base rate is n=1 for shipping incidents and n=0 for escalation, too thin to size a positive-EV trade. The prior analogue's 1-day Brent reaction was negative, which argues against an outright long. Tanker equities (FRO -10.2%, STNG -10.7%, DHT -6.9% over 5 days) already moved before the news and offer no clean reaction signal. Attribution is unconfirmed and no live AIS data is available. Revisit once the day-one price reaction and any official attribution or follow-on incidents are visible.

rows.title: IRGC seizes the tanker Stena Impero in the Strait of Hormuz
rows.regime: Elevated Gulf maritime risk after the IRGC seizure of a tanker in Hormuz, with a sharp prior sell-off in crude and no confirmed escalation beyond this seizure.

trades.thesis: A state seizure in Hormuz after two prior tanker attacks should lift the geopolitical risk premium for several sessions, and the recent 6% five-day sell-off leaves room for a partial rebound.

rows.title: Drone and missile strike on Saudi Abqaiq and Khurais (5.7 mb/d offline)
rows.regime: Acute supply shock: a large, sudden Saudi crude outage (5.7 mb/d reported offline) on a Saturday gap, with no reopening price yet in the data.
rows.noTrade: No tanker equity trade: FRO and STNG already rallied 40%+ over 20 days, so the supply view is priced in and equities carry idiosyncratic freight risk. No product or spread trade: the crack and Brent-WTI analogues are thin and the outage hits crude first. No short trade: no evidence yet supports a fade beyond the reversal tendency that the 20-day base rate already reflects.

trades.thesis: A reported 5.7 mb/d outage is far larger than any prior incident in the sample, so the first-week price response should exceed the shipping-family 5-day median, before any restoration or stock-release response fades it.

rows.title: US strike kills IRGC commander Qassem Soleimani
rows.regime: Geopolitical risk spike in the Gulf after a state-level strike; no live vessel data, so the read rests on headlines, prices and a thin event study.
rows.noTrade: No tanker equity (FRO, DHT, STNG) or spread trade: the shipping-family equity base rates are contradictory across horizons (20d medians negative) and the sample is too small to size them. Gold and products are excluded because the link to the event is weaker and the evidence is thin.

trades.thesis: Retaliation risk against Gulf energy infrastructure or tankers raises the near-term risk premium in Brent, which typically shows up within a few sessions of a state-level strike.

rows.title: Iran fires missiles at US bases in Iraq
rows.regime: Geopolitical risk spike after a direct Iran-to-US strike, with no confirmed shipping or supply disruption yet
rows.noTrade: Single-day missile strike with no reported shipping, Hormuz or supply impact; the escalation base rate (n=2) is too thin to give a positive expected value after costs at a probability I can defend. Brent already reflects about +6% over 20 days, and the prior shipping-family 20-day moves were mostly negative. Revisit on confirmed casualties, a tanker incident, or a Hormuz transit disruption.

rows.title: Drone strike on the tanker Mercer Street off Oman
rows.regime: Elevated Hormuz maritime risk after a single-vessel drone strike, with attribution and supply impact unconfirmed.
rows.noTrade: Three shipping-family incidents and three escalation-family incidents are too few to separate a persistent premium from a transient spike, and the two families point in opposite directions beyond 1 to 5 days. The event carries no verified supply impact, and attribution rests on unverified sources. Tanker equities (FRO, DHT, STNG) have already sold off sharply over 20 days, so their reaction is ambiguous. Expected value after costs cannot be shown with honest probabilities above 0.5, so no paper position is justified yet. Revisit if the incident broadens to additional vessels, a cargo or crew loss, or a verified throughput disruption through Hormuz.

rows.title: Hamas attack on Israel; regional war risk
rows.regime: Geopolitical shock to a market already in a bearish trend: Brent down 11.3% over 5 days and 6.7% over 20 days into the 2023-10-07 news, with no verified supply or shipping disruption yet.
rows.noTrade: No edge we can defend. The only shock-type signal in the history is a short-lived 1-day spike that fades within 5-20 days, which argues against a directional trade. The evidence is thin: no vessel data, no confirmed flow disruption, and the Brent-WTI and tanker moves are too small to size against a 2.7% daily Brent standard deviation. Any positive expected value we could state would rest on probabilities we cannot support, so we stay flat.

rows.title: Houthis seize the car carrier Galaxy Leader in the Red Sea
rows.regime: Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb maritime risk is elevated after a state-linked seizure, but crude is in a 20-day downtrend and the escalation base rate is small and mixed.

trades.thesis: A state-linked seizure in the Red Sea raises near-term freight and risk premia, so a short-lived Brent bid is plausible over the next few sessions. Size is kept small because the 20-day trend is down and the event may be partly priced.

rows.title: Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd pause Red Sea transits; BP follows
rows.regime: Shipping-disruption shock in the Red Sea: a major liner pause that is a corporate routing decision, not a confirmed attack, so the price impact is still uncertain.
rows.noTrade: Crude and Brent-WTI are not traded: the Brent shipping-family edge (5d median +1.6%, 3/5 up) is too thin after costs against a 2.7% daily s.d., and the Brent-WTI and crack legs have no direct evidence. No vessel data is available to confirm the disruption, so I hold size to one small tanker-equity idea.

trades.thesis: Longer Cape routings absorb tanker capacity, which should lift crude tanker earnings and equities over the next two weeks. FRO has already fallen about 13% over 20 days, so the reversal case is not fully priced.

rows.title: US and UK strike Houthi targets in Yemen
rows.regime: Elevated Red Sea geopolitical risk after a US/UK strike on Houthi targets, with no measurable price confirmation yet and a thin, mixed base rate.
rows.noTrade: Base rates are small (n=6 shipping, n=4 escalation) and mixed: the 1-5 day Brent drift is positive but weak, while the 20-day medians are negative in both families. The event is a retaliatory strike rather than a supply loss, and the Brent move is unconfirmed. Honest probabilities sit near 0.50-0.52, which does not clear costs at sensible stop and target sizes. The escalation family's negative 20-day Brent median argues against a longer-dated long. No vessel data is available (none is live), so the AIS picture cannot support a shipping trade.

rows.title: Houthi missile sets the tanker Marlin Luanda on fire
rows.regime: Elevated Red Sea escalation risk after a single breaking headline; prices already up sharply over 5 days.
rows.noTrade: Only one unconfirmed headline with no vessel, AIS or official confirmation in the input, and no live vessel data. Prices already reflect a 5-6% five-day rally, and the incremental news is partly priced in given the prior Red Sea campaign. Historical samples are too small (5-6 events per bucket) to support probabilities clearly above 0.5 after costs, and the 20-day base-rate medians fade for crude and tanker equities. I would rather wait for confirmation of the incident and any supply or freight impact before risking paper capital.

rows.title: Iran's drone and missile attack on Israel; IRGC seizes MSC Aries near Hormuz
rows.regime: Acute geopolitical risk spike over a weekend, with Monday gap risk and no live vessel data

trades.thesis: The seizure of a merchant vessel near Hormuz plus a direct Iran-Israel strike raises the risk premium on crude over the next week, and Brent should gap up at the Monday open and hold part of it.
Crude tanker equities usually re-rate when Hormuz transit risk rises, and FRO has the most consistent 5-day up bias in the shipping family.

rows.title: Israeli strike near Isfahan, Iran
rows.regime: Geopolitical headline shock in the Middle East with no verified follow-through; price reaction is unconfirmed and the event study is too thin to size a trade.
rows.noTrade: Only one unverified headline with no scale, damage, or response detail. The escalation base rate rests on six incidents and reverses over 5 and 20 days, so any edge I could state would be within noise. Shipping-family data shows no clear tanker or product-tanker signal, and AIS data is unavailable. Revisit once there is a confirmed Iranian response, a shipping or Hormuz-specific disruption, or a clear multi-day price reaction.

rows.title: Houthis attack the tanker Sounion (1m bbl) in the Red Sea
rows.regime: Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb attack risk on a falling-price crude market; a single tanker strike, not a sustained supply outage.

trades.thesis: A tanker strike in the Red Sea lengthens voyages and tightens crude tanker supply, which should lift Frontline's earnings expectations over the next week.

rows.title: Iran fires ~180 ballistic missiles at Israel
rows.regime: Geopolitical event shock: direct Iran-Israel missile exchange, with no post-news price data and no live vessel data.
rows.noTrade: No verified post-news price or entry level, so the edge cannot be sized. The escalation base rates are small-sample and mixed: the 1-day lift is roughly a coin flip (4/7 up) and the 20-day reading reverses. No live vessel data is available, so the shipping-disruption channel is unconfirmed. Revisit once post-news prices and tanker movements through Hormuz are observable.

rows.title: Israel strikes Iran, avoiding oil infrastructure
rows.regime: Geopolitical risk premium elevated after a headline Israel-Iran strike; no tanker or shipping disruption confirmed
rows.noTrade: Only one unverified headline; the strike explicitly avoids oil infrastructure, so the supply channel is weak. No state-strike base rate for prices, no live AIS data, and the escalation-family evidence (Brent 1d median +0.8%, 5 of 8 up) is too thin to produce positive expected value after costs. Wait for confirmed shipping or infrastructure impact or a clear follow-up strike pattern.

rows.title: Israel launches strikes on Iran's nuclear and military sites
rows.regime: Geopolitical risk premium in crude after a sharp run-up; no confirmed supply or shipping disruption yet.
rows.noTrade: No edge after costs. The news is a state-strike rather than a shipping or supply event, and the escalation base rates are weak (n=9) and do not support a 20-day upside. Brent is already up about 15% in 20 days, so a long chase risks buying the peak. There is no live AIS data to confirm any Hormuz disruption, and the 1-day reaction is unknown. Revisit if vessel or flow data shows actual disruption, or if a price reversal gives a defined setup.

rows.title: US strikes Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan
rows.regime: Acute geopolitical escalation with no observed shipping impact yet; the price move is largely priced in from the prior two weeks.
rows.noTrade: No edge I can state with confidence. There is no live AIS or vessel data, so I cannot observe a shipping disruption. The event is a nuclear-site strike, not a tanker or chokepoint incident, and the closest analogues (escalation family, n=10) show a near-zero 1-day Brent median and a negative 20-day median with only 3 of 10 up. Brent is already up about 11% in five sessions, so a long chases a move that may already be priced, and a short against an unresolved retaliation risk has no clear entry or stop. Stops sized to Brent's 2.7% daily volatility would also make any edge small relative to costs. I would wait for confirmed shipping impact or a clearer post-news price reaction before proposing a paper trade.

rows.title: Houthis sink the bulkers Magic Seas and Eternity C
rows.regime: Headline-driven Red Sea risk with no confirmed crude-supply impact; Brent is near $68 after a 20-day rise of about 5%.
rows.noTrade: The trigger is an unverified breaking headline about dry bulkers, not tankers or crude flows. The base rates are mixed to negative for Brent, WTI and the tanker equities over 1 to 5 days, and the samples are small. No live vessel data is available, so I cannot confirm any disruption to tanker traffic. Wait for official confirmation, a named source, or tanker-specific incidents before risking capital.
